summary: This unit teaches you to develop a business plan that a bank, an investor, a fund or your own management team can use. You will learn the purpose and the parts of a plan, how to describe the business and choose its legal structure, how to analyse the market, plan operations and people, build the financial forecasts (start-up costs, sales, income statement, cash flow and break-even), deal with risk, set a timeline, tailor and present the plan, and keep it up to date as a working document.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers who must write, review or use a business plan: for a new business, a new branch, a loan application or a grant. A business plan sets out **what the business will do, for whom, how, with what money and by when**. It is a tool for thinking and for persuading, and later a standard to measure results against.

A plan is only as good as its evidence and its figures. A plan that doubles the sales forecast to win a loan may win the loan, but the owner will then struggle to repay it, and the lender may lose trust. Plans must be realistic, evidence-based and clearly written.

Explain premises, production or service delivery, suppliers, capacity, management and staffing, and how the brand and recipes or designs are protected.

Manage risk and set a timeline
Identify risks and contingency plans, and set an action plan with owners, deadlines and milestones.
Write a clear executive summary, tailor the plan for each reader, protect confidential material, and review and update the plan.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario and calculation questions, including start-up costs, forecasts, profit, break-even, cash flow and ratios.
A **written paper** of short answers (exact terms such as collateral, milestone, sole trader) and essays.
**Practical group work**: writing the main sections of a plan for a made-up venture, then preparing the financial plan in a spreadsheet and defending it before a loan panel.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and say which year or month your figure covers. Many marks are lost on a correct method with a wrong period.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The purpose, the readers and the planning process

ul: To **set goals and the way to reach them**.
To test the idea on paper before spending real money.
To raise finance: lenders, investors and funds ask for a plan.
To guide the owner and staff, and to measure progress once the business is trading.

blocks.p: Know your reader. A **bank** lends money that must be repaid with interest: it looks hardest at whether cash flow can repay the loan, and at the owner's own investment, the security offered and the experience of the team. An **equity investor** takes a share of ownership and wants to see growth and what share and say the investor will get. A **grant fund** wants to see how the project meets its criteria. **Your own managers** want targets, tasks and deadlines.

flow: Be clear on the purpose of the plan and its readers
Gather information: market research, quotations for equipment and premises, licence and legal requirements, and cost and price information
Set the vision, mission and objectives, and decide the strategy, using a SWOT analysis of the findings
Draft each section: marketing, operations, management, financial plan and risks
Ask an accountant and a few experienced business people to review it, to catch weak assumptions and gaps early
Revise, write the executive summary last, proofread and finalise

blocks.note: Write the executive summary **last**, because it sums up everything else. Keep the plan concise: put detailed data, such as quotations and survey tables, in the appendices.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A business plan is written before the business has real results, so many figures are informed estimates. Once the business trades, actual sales, costs and customer responses will differ. A plan that is filed away cannot tell the owner whether the business is on track. Used as a **working document**, it gives targets to measure against: check results against targets every month, ask why any gap exists, and update the plan with actual results and new forecasts.

sections.title: Describing the business: vision, objectives and legal structure

head: Term
What it says
Example for a small guest house
rows: Where the business aims to be in the long term
To be the best-known small guest house in its parish
What the business does, for whom and how, today
To give visitors clean, friendly rooms with local food at fair prices
Measurable targets for the plan period
Reach 65% average occupancy and a guest rating of at least 9 out of 10 by the end of year two
The main ways the objectives will be achieved
Partner with two tour operators; train staff in guest care; add an online booking page

blocks.p: Good objectives are **SMART**: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. "To sell J$15 million in year two" is easy to monitor; "to do well" is not. A community group or social enterprise that reinvests its profits in training should have both **financial and social targets**.

blocks.note: Link the chain: the vision is shaped by the owner, the objectives turn it into numbers, and the strategies are built on the SWOT findings: use strengths to meet opportunities and fix weaknesses.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Structure
Who owns it
Liability
Points to note
rows: **Unlimited**: the owner is personally liable for all debts
Simplest and cheapest; the owner keeps all profit and control; hard to raise large sums
Two or more people sharing skills, money and work
Usually **unlimited**; each partner may be bound by the others' business decisions
Needs a written partnership agreement on profit shares, decisions and duties; disputes can end it
**Limited** to the money put in for the shares, in general
Registration under company law and more reporting; easier to bring in investors; lenders may still ask owners for personal guarantees

blocks.p: Which structure should the plan propose? If the owners want to protect their personal assets from the business's debts and may want to bring in new investors later, a limited liability company is usually the better choice. Where owners keep it small and informal, a sole trader or partnership may do. State the reason, and take advice on registration and tax.

blocks.note: Some forms of business must be registered, for example a company under company law, and tax registration may be needed, including GCT where it applies. The plan should list the registrations and who will complete them, not quote section numbers or penalties.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Market analysis, competitive advantage and marketing

blocks.p: The market analysis proves that demand is real. Use **research data** on customers, market size and competitors, not opinions or the owner's belief. Include:

ul: **Target customers:** who they are, where they live and what they need.
**Market size and trends:** how many customers and how much they spend, and whether the market is growing.
**Competitors:** who they are, their prices, strengths and weaknesses.
**PESTLE and SWOT findings** that shape the strategy.

blocks.p: The competitive advantage section must show **why customers will choose the firm over rivals**: quality, speed, location, price, service or a skill nobody else has. State it as a customer benefit and show the evidence. Be careful with price. A café that sets prices just below a nearby rival's, when its own costs are higher, may fail to cover its costs and earn a profit. Being cheaper is only an advantage if the margin still works.

head: Part
What the plan should say
rows: What is offered, its features and its USP
The price, how it was set (costs, rivals, what customers will pay), and discounts
Where and how customers buy: shop, online, delivery, through retailers; why the location was chosen, because it affects sales, costs and access
How customers will hear: social media, posters, radio, word of mouth, partners; with a budget
Who the marketing is aimed at, from the market analysis
The cost of each activity and what it should achieve

blocks.p: Match channels to customers and cost. Targeted social media posts reach young adults cheaply; a notice in a church bulletin may suit another group. The plan should say how it will measure whether each activity works.

sections.title: Operations, management and protecting the business

blocks.p: The operations section tells the reader **how the product is made or the service is delivered**. A bank wants to know that the business can really do what the plan says.

head: Topic
What to describe
rows: Size, access for delivery vehicles, power and water, why the site was chosen, rent or purchase
Machines and tools, their cost, capacity and who will maintain them
The steps from raw material or enquiry to finished product or service
Main suppliers, prices, lead times and back-up suppliers
How much the business can produce or serve in a week or month, and what limits it
Checks, standards, health and safety, and licences

blocks.p: Lenders and investors look closely at the management section because **the team must be able to deliver the plan**. Show the owners' and managers' experience and qualifications, the roles, and any skills missing. If nobody has accounting experience, say how the gap will be filled: a part-time accountant, a trained bookkeeper or a short course.

When the plan says it will hire staff, the financial section must include their **wages and statutory contributions**, not just wages. For example, a plan to hire eight staff in the first month must show the payroll cost every month from then on, with the deductions and employer contributions that the law requires.

ul: **Brand:** a new brand name, such as for a pepper sauce, can be protected by registering it as a trade mark. First check that no one else already holds it.
**Recipes and designs:** keep them confidential and limit who knows them; use written agreements with staff and partners.
**Insurance:** cover for property, stock and liability that the business needs.
**Confidentiality when sharing the plan:** ask each possible investor to sign a confidentiality agreement before they read it.

blocks.note: The plan itself can contain sensitive ideas and figures. Mark it confidential, number the copies and record who has each copy.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The financial plan: start-up costs, funding and forecasts

blocks.p: The financial plan turns the whole plan into money. It must be consistent with the other sections, show its **assumptions**, and give the same figures to every reader.

blocks.h: Start-up costs and sources of funds

blocks.p: List every cost of getting started, including working capital to run the business until sales arrive, then show where each dollar will come from.

Total costs must equal total funds. The owners put in J$1,000,000, so the other funding needed is 2,600,000 − 1,000,000 = **J$1,600,000**. The **debt-to-equity ratio** is debt ÷ equity = 1,600,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = **1.6 : 1**. A high ratio means the business relies heavily on borrowing and is riskier for a lender.
**Interest** on a simple-interest loan = amount × rate × years. At 10% a year, one year's interest on J$1,600,000 is 1,600,000 × 0.10 = J$160,000.

blocks.note: **Collateral** is an asset that a borrower pledges to a lender in case a loan is not repaid. Lenders usually also want to see that the owners have put in their own money. An investor offering money for a share of the business needs the plan to state what share and what say the investor will get.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Build the sales forecast from facts, not hope: the number of customers or orders × the average price × the number of periods. For example, 120 customers a week × J$1,800 × 50 trading weeks = J$10,800,000 a year. Show it month by month for the first year (seasonal businesses will not sell evenly) and then year by year. If sales grow by a stated percentage, apply it to the previous year: J$8,000,000 growing by 25% a year gives J$10,000,000 in year two and J$12,500,000 in year three.

A list of **key assumptions** lets readers test the forecast: the price, the customers per week, the cost of materials, the exchange rate for imported items, the payment terms customers get. If the assumptions are not shown, the figures cannot be checked.

blocks.note: If the business is registered for GCT, show sales **before** GCT in the forecast and plan to pay the GCT collected over to the tax authority. GCT is not income of the business. Use the current rate and do not quote a figure in the plan unless it is checked.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The financial plan: profit, cash flow and break-even

blocks.p: The income statement shows the expected profit for a period: sales less costs.

head: Line
How it is worked out
J$
rows: Wages, rent, power, loan interest, insurance and other fixed costs

blocks.p: Profit is not cash. Customers may pay late, stock must be bought before it is sold, and loan repayments and equipment are paid out of cash but do not all appear as costs in the income statement. The **cash flow forecast** shows, month by month, the cash coming in and going out and the balance in the bank.

Closing balance = opening balance + cash in − cash out. The closing balance of one month is the opening balance of the next. Month 3 shows a negative balance of J$300,000. Even if the year's profit is good, the plan must **arrange funding for those months**, such as an overdraft limit of at least that amount with some margin, and say when it will be repaid.

A lender also compares **monthly net cash from trading** with **monthly loan repayments**. If trading gives J$140,000 a month and the repayment is J$110,000, the business can repay but with little margin: a small fall in sales could cause a missed payment.

**Break-even sales** = fixed costs ÷ contribution ratio, where the contribution ratio is the contribution per J$1 of sales. If fixed costs are J$4,500,000 a year and each J$1 of sales gives 60 cents of contribution, break-even sales = 4,500,000 ÷ 0.60 = **J$7,500,000**. Check: 60% of 7,500,000 = 4,500,000.
Show what happens to profit if sales are 10% lower than forecast, so the reader sees how the business copes. Variable costs fall with sales, but fixed costs do not, so profit falls by more than 10%.

ul: Sales J$16,000,000; variable costs 40% of sales; fixed costs J$5,000,000.
Sales fell 10% but profit fell by about 21% (960,000 ÷ 4,600,000), because the fixed costs stayed the same.

blocks.note: The common mistake is to take 10% off the profit. Take 10% off the sales, then work out the profit again with the fixed costs unchanged.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Risk, contingency and the implementation timeline

blocks.p: The risk section lists what could stop the business reaching its objectives, how likely each is, how serious its effect would be, and what the owner will do. Use the SWOT and PESTLE findings and talk to experienced people. A small farm that supplies hotels might list drought (response: irrigation and storage), a hurricane (insurance and a reserve), the loss of its biggest customer (a wider customer list) and rising feed or fuel costs (contracts and efficiency).

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Response
rows: Irrigation, water storage, crop insurance where available
Loss of the biggest hotel customer
Win at least three more regular buyers; keep a cash reserve
Agree payment terms; invoice promptly; chase early
Servicing plan; a spare supplier of repairs

blocks.p: A **contingency plan** sets out what the firm will do if key risks happen, for example the steps, who is responsible and where the money comes from. Plan for the worst, but show the reader that you have thought about it, not that you expect it.

blocks.h: The implementation timeline and action plan

blocks.p: The timeline turns the plan into dated steps. A **milestone** is a key event with a target date, such as "premises fitted out and opened by 1 March". An **action plan** states, for each key task, the **owner, the deadline and the resources**.

head: Task
Owner
Deadline
Resources
Milestone
rows: Register the business and get licences

blocks.p: Keep the business on track with **monthly checks of results against targets**, rather than waiting until the end of the year.

sections.title: Writing, presenting and using the plan

head: Section
What it does for the reader
rows: Key points of the plan and the funding sought; written last
Vision, mission, objectives and legal structure
Evidence of demand, rivals and why customers will choose you
How it will be delivered and who will do it
Start-up costs, funding, forecasts, cash flow, break-even and assumptions
What could go wrong and what you will do
Quotations, CVs, survey results, licences, detailed tables

blocks.p: Use headings, page numbers and a contents list so a loan officer can find a section quickly. Use plain language and short paragraphs.

blocks.h: Tailor the plan to the reader

blocks.p: The facts and figures must be **the same** for every reader: honesty matters and readers may compare versions. What changes is the emphasis and the level of detail.

head: Reader
What they care about most
rows: Safety: cash flow to repay the loan, repayments in quiet months, security offered, the owners' own investment, the team's experience
Growth and return: the size of the market, the competitive advantage, the share of ownership offered, how and when the investor can exit
How the project meets the fund's stated criteria and priorities
Targets, tasks, owners, deadlines and monthly measures

ul: Keep forecasts realistic and evidence-based. Do not inflate sales to win approval, even if an adviser suggests it.
State assumptions and risks plainly.
Respect confidentiality: use agreements when sharing the plan with several possible investors.
Do not quote the work of others without crediting them.

blocks.p: An **elevator pitch** is a short spoken summary of the plan, brief enough to give in about a minute: who the customers are, what the business offers, why it will win, how much money is needed and what it will earn. Practise it, so that you can use any chance to speak to a lender or an investor.

ul: explain the purpose of a business plan and who reads it.
follow the process of developing a plan, including consulting and review.
write a vision, a mission and SMART objectives, including social objectives where relevant.

calculate start-up costs, other funding needed, the debt-to-equity ratio and simple interest.
build a sales forecast and a list of key assumptions.
prepare an income statement and calculate gross profit, net profit and net profit margin.
prepare a cash flow forecast and arrange funding for negative months.

terms: A document setting out what a business will do, how, with what money and by when.
Where the business aims to be in the long term.
What the business does, for whom and how, today.
A measurable target for the plan period.
A business owned and run by one person, who is personally liable for all its debts.
A written document on how partners share profits, decisions and duties.
A company whose owners' liability is limited to the money they put in.
The short section at the front that sums up the whole plan.
All the costs of getting the business ready to trade.
Cash needed to pay running costs until sales bring in money.
Money put in by the owners or investors in return for ownership.
Money borrowed, to be repaid with interest.

The plan's estimate of future sales.

c1.title: A signage shop in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: Two partners plan a printing and signage shop in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. Their start-up costs are: printing machine J$3,200,000; shop fit-out J$800,000; opening stock of materials J$500,000; licences and deposits J$250,000; and working capital J$750,000. They will put in J$2,200,000 of their own money and borrow the rest from a bank at 11% simple interest a year.

c2.title: A laundromat in Portmore
c2.text: A business plan for a laundromat in Portmore forecasts 80 loads a day at J$700 a load, over 300 trading days in the year. Variable costs (water, power and detergent) are 30% of sales. Fixed costs are J$8,400,000 a year.

c3.title: A poultry farm that supplies hotels
c3.text: Garfield Ellis plans to expand his poultry farm in Clarendon, selling to hotels that pay 30 to 60 days after delivery. His plan shows a profit of J$1,600,000 for the year. His cash flow forecast starts with J$400,000 in the bank. Month 1: cash in J$900,000 and cash out J$1,350,000. Month 2: cash in J$1,100,000 and cash out J$1,200,000. Month 3: cash in J$1,800,000 and cash out J$1,300,000.

c4.title: Two sisters and a catering business
c4.text: Joy and Pauline Walker plan a catering business in Brown's Town, St Ann. Pauline can put in less money than Joy and does not want her house to be at risk if the business fails. They may bring in a third owner later. Neither sister has any accounting experience.

c5.title: A tailor's plan in Linstead
c5.text: Opal Reid started a school-uniform tailoring business in Linstead, St Catherine, using a business plan. For the latest month, the plan forecast sales of J$1,500,000, but actual sales were J$1,320,000. Three possible investors have asked to see the plan, and one of them has asked how the sales forecast was worked out.

questions.q: How much do the partners need to borrow?
What is the debt-to-equity ratio of the start-up funding?
questions.why: Debt ÷ equity = 3,300,000 ÷ 2,200,000 = 1.5, so 1.5 : 1. Inverting the ratio gives 0.67 : 1. Dividing total funds by equity (2.5) is not the debt-to-equity ratio.

questions.q: What is the interest on the loan for one year?
questions.why: Simple interest = 3,300,000 × 0.11 = J$363,000. Using the total costs (J$605,000) or the owners' money (J$242,000) uses the wrong amount. Check: 10% would be 330,000, so 11% must be a little more.

questions.q: Why does the plan include J$750,000 of working capital?
o: To buy the printing machine at a discount
To repay the first year's bank interest in advance
To pay running costs until sales bring in money
To act as security for the bank loan
questions.why: A new business has costs from day one but sales arrive later. Working capital covers wages, rent and materials in the gap. Without it the business can run out of cash even if the plan is sound.

questions.q: What is the laundromat's yearly sales forecast?
questions.why: 80 loads × J$700 = J$56,000 a day. J$56,000 × 300 days = J$16,800,000. J$56,000 is only one day; J$1,400,000 is one month of 25 days.

questions.q: What are the laundromat's total variable costs for the year?
questions.why: Variable costs are 30% of sales: 16,800,000 × 0.30 = J$5,040,000. Taking them from sales leaves a contribution of J$11,760,000, and after the fixed costs of J$8,400,000 the net profit is J$3,360,000. J$13,440,000 wrongly adds fixed and variable costs together.

questions.q: What yearly sales does the laundromat need to break even?
questions.why: Contribution ratio = 70% (100% − 30%). Break-even = 8,400,000 ÷ 0.70 = J$12,000,000. Check: 70% of 12,000,000 = 8,400,000. Dividing by 0.30 would give J$28,000,000, which is wrong.

questions.q: If demand falls to 70 loads a day and nothing else changes, what is the yearly net profit?
questions.why: Sales = 70 × 700 × 300 = 14,700,000. Variable costs at 30% = 4,410,000, so the contribution is 10,290,000. Less fixed costs of 8,400,000 = J$1,890,000. Taking 12.5% off the profit (J$2,940,000) forgets that fixed costs stay the same.

questions.q: How much will the farm have in the bank at the end of month 3?
o: J$150,000 overdrawn
J$350,000 in credit
J$1,800,000 in credit
J$500,000 in credit
questions.why: Month 1 ends at −50,000 (400,000 + 900,000 − 1,350,000). Month 2 ends at −150,000. Month 3 ends at −150,000 + 1,800,000 − 1,300,000 = +J$350,000. Each month's closing balance is the next month's opening balance.

questions.q: What is the largest amount of overdraft the farm needs in months 1 to 3?
questions.why: Month 2 closing = −50,000 + 1,100,000 − 1,200,000 = −150,000. Month 3 closing = −150,000 + 1,800,000 − 1,300,000 = +350,000. The lowest point is −J$150,000, so he needs at least that, plus a margin.

questions.q: What should the plan do about the negative balances?
o: Arrange funding such as an overdraft for months 1 and 2
Show only the yearly profit so that the plan looks sound
Raise the sales forecast so that the balance is positive
Ask the hotels to pay in 90 days instead
questions.why: A plan must show how the gap will be funded, with the amount and the date of repayment. Hiding the problem or changing the figures without evidence misleads the lender, and longer terms would make the gap worse.

questions.q: The plan shows a good profit for the year. Why must it still show cash flow month by month?
o: Profit and cash flow always give exactly the same figures
Lenders read only the cash flow and ignore the profit
The cash flow forecast takes the place of the income statement
Cash can go out before it comes in, even in a profitable year
questions.why: Profit measures the year's earnings; cash flow shows timing. Payment terms, stock and loan repayments can leave the bank balance negative in some months, which a lender will check.

questions.q: Which legal structure best suits the sisters' wishes?
o: A sole trader business owned by Joy
A partnership with no written agreement
A partnership with unlimited liability for both
A limited liability company
questions.why: A limited company limits the owners' liability to the money they put in (in general) and makes it easier to bring in a third owner later. Sole trader and partnership owners are usually personally liable for the debts.

questions.q: If they choose a partnership instead, what document should they write?
o: An executive summary of the partnership's plans
A partnership agreement on profit shares and duties
A cash flow forecast for the first year only
A contingency plan for each of the business's risks
questions.why: A partnership agreement sets out how profits are shared, how decisions are made, what each partner does and what happens if one leaves. Without one, disputes can end the business.

questions.q: In a partnership, what is usually the position of the partners if the business cannot pay its debts?
o: They lose only the money they put into the business
Only the partner who signed the loan is liable
They are usually personally liable for the debts
The bank must write off the debt owed to it
questions.why: Partners usually have unlimited liability, and one partner's business decisions can bind the others. A limited company is the structure that normally limits liability.

questions.q: The management section shows nobody with accounting experience. What should the plan do?
o: Show how it will fill the gap, for example with an accountant
Leave the gap out, because lenders only read the financial plan
Say that Joy will learn bookkeeping when the business is open
State that accounting will not be needed in the first year
questions.why: Lenders and investors look at the management section to see that the team can deliver the plan. Naming the gap and the solution, such as a part-time accountant or trained bookkeeper, builds confidence.

questions.q: By how much were Opal's actual sales below the forecast for the month?
o: J$180,000, which is 12% of the forecast
J$180,000, which is 13.6% of the forecast
J$1,320,000, which is 88% of the forecast
J$150,000, which is 10% of the forecast
questions.why: Variance = 1,500,000 − 1,320,000 = J$180,000. As a percentage of the forecast, 180,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 12%. Dividing by the actual figure (13.6%) is a common mistake.

questions.q: What should Opal do with her plan when sales fall short?
o: Keep the plan unchanged, because it was approved
Replace the plan with a new one each week
Hide the gap until the end of the year
Find the cause of the gap and update the plan
questions.why: A plan is a working document. Comparing actual results with targets, asking why, and updating forecasts keeps it useful for decisions, and lenders and investors expect an owner to know the gap.

questions.q: An investor asks how the sales forecast was worked out. What should Opal do?
o: Say that the figures are confidential
Show the assumptions behind it, such as orders and price
Offer a higher forecast to impress the investor
Tell the investor the figures came from an experienced adviser
questions.why: Stating assumptions lets readers test the forecast, which builds trust. Forecasts built from evidence such as orders, prices and market research are more credible than a figure that cannot be explained.

questions.q: A plan sets fixed costs at J$2,400,000 a year, a price of J$1,500 and a variable cost of J$900 a unit. How many units must be sold in a year to break even?
o: 1,600 units
2,667 units
4,000 units
6,000 units
questions.why: Contribution = 1,500 − 900 = J$600 a unit. Break-even = 2,400,000 ÷ 600 = 4,000 units. Check: 4,000 × 600 = 2,400,000. Dividing by the price gives 1,600 and dividing by the variable cost gives 2,667; both are wrong.
